note: Proposed Canadian historiography group entries. Anchor people are names as they appear in ../canadian-historiography-scholars-request-2026-10-12/candidates.csv. A person may anchor more than one group (rosters are not edges); 'primary' marks where their person entry would attach. Scope notes are editorial drafts, not sourced descriptions.

groups.label: Laurentian school & the national tradition
groups.scope: Staples and Laurentian interpretations (Innis, Creighton), metropolitanism (Careless), and the political-national synthesis of the Centenary Series; the tradition Berger's Writing of Canadian History (1976) analyses.

groups.label: English-Canadian intellectual & cultural history
groups.scope: Ideas of nation, empire and reform (Berger, Cook), the intellectuals of the state (Owram), antimodernism and the invented folk (McKay), pageantry, myth and memory (Nelles, Francis, Vance, Coates).

groups.label: Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada
groups.scope: The social gospel and the 'regenerators' (Allen, Cook), the secularization debate (Christie and Gauvreau against Cook and Marshall), Catholicism and the Quiet Revolution, religion and everyday life.

groups.label: Liberal order framework
groups.scope: McKay's prospectus (2000) for reading Canada as a liberal project of rule, closer to a history of capitalism than to moral regulation: the spread of a liberal order of property, individualism and market relations, its state-formation roots (Greer and Radforth 1992, Curtis 2001), and its debate (Constant and Ducharme 2009).
groups.decision: Kept separate from moral regulation: "a different project closer to history of capitalism" (user, 2026-10-12). No international history-of-capitalism entry; the fields haven't connected, so the link is not forced (user, 2026-10-12).

groups.label: Moral regulation & the regulatory state
groups.scope: Moral reform, sexuality, law and the 'psy' sciences as instruments of governance: Valverde's Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991), the national-security campaign against queers (Kinsman), eugenics (McLaren), the 'girl problem' (Strange), normality (Gleason, Adams).

groups.label: Canadian working-class history
groups.scope: The new labour history of the 1970s (Kealey, Palmer, Labour/Le Travail 1976) against an older institutional labour history (Bercuson), poverty and the welfare state (Copp, Struthers, Finkel), deindustrialization (High).

groups.label: Canadian women's & gender history
groups.scope: From recovering women's lives (Prentice, Strong-Boag, Pierson, Mitchinson) to gender as a category of class, family and state (Parr, Bradbury, Sangster, Iacovetta), masculinity and the gendered languages of politics (Morgan), postwar domesticity and consumption (Korinek, Fahrni, Campbell).

groups.label: Childhood, youth & family in Canada
groups.scope: Children, adolescence and family as subjects of reform and expertise: youth and modernity (Comacchio), the psy-sciences and normal families (Gleason), postwar youth and heterosexuality (Adams), the baby boom (Owram).
groups.decision: Its own entry, a topic field (user, 2026-10-12).

groups.label: Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada
groups.scope: Immigrant workers and 'dangerous foreigners' (Avery), immigrant women and Cold War reception (Iacovetta), ethnic identity (Swyripa, Perin), policy (Knowles), and the history of racism and whiteness (Ward, Roy, Backhouse, Walker on the Black Loyalists).

groups.label: Native–newcomer relations & fur-trade history
groups.scope: From Innis's fur trade to Indigenous people as actors: trading strategies (Ray), fur-trade families (Van Kirk, Brown), the Huron (Trigger), policy and treaties (Miller, Carter), residential schools (Milloy), health and bodies (Kelm), encounter and labour (Raibmon, Lutz), voyageurs (Podruchny).

groups.label: Quebec historiography
groups.scope: From Groulx and the Montreal and Laval schools to the 'modernist' or revisionist synthesis (Linteau, Durocher, Robert), its critique (Rudin 1997), comparative and intellectual histories (Bouchard, Lamonde), and the Quiet Revolution's origins (Behiels, Gauvreau).

groups.label: Canadian military history: official history, war & society, memory
groups.scope: Official history (Stacey), the war-and-society turn (Morton, Copp), the home front (Keshen, Rutherdale), memory and myth (Vance, Cook), and popular military history (Berton).

groups.label: Political, international & national history
groups.scope: Political and diplomatic history of the state, mandarins and foreign policy (Granatstein, Bothwell, English, Hillmer, Whitaker), Canada and the British World (Buckner, Francis), national syntheses, and business and economic biography (Bliss).
groups.decision: The "Who Killed Canadian History?" debate is a separate entry (user, 2026-10-12).

groups.label: The 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate
groups.scope: The 1990s quarrel over national history: Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' (1991) and Granatstein's Who Killed Canadian History? (1998) charged social historians with fragmenting the national story; responses defended social, gender, labour and regional history (Kealey 1992, McKillop 1999, and later Dummitt and Dawson's Contesting Clio's Craft, 2009). Its roots lie in the 'limited identities' argument (Careless 1969; Buckner 2000).

groups.label: Regionalism & limited identities: the West, the Atlantic, British Columbia
groups.scope: Careless's 'limited identities' (1969) and the regional histories that followed: the Prairies (Morton, Friesen, Waiser), the Atlantic (Acadiensis 1971, Conrad, Reid), British Columbia (Barman), rural society (Sandwell).

groups.label: Canada's 1960s
groups.scope: The Sixties as their own historiographical subject: the baby boom (Owram 1996), English Canada's 'other Quiet Revolution' (Igartua 2006), the New Left, youth and dissent (Palmer 2009; Campbell, Clément and Kealey's Debating Dissent, 2012), decolonization and Montreal radicalism (Mills 2010), and the rights revolution (Clément).
groups.decision: Replaces the "postwar Canada" data cluster: "1960s is its own thing" (user, 2026-10-12).

environment.note: No separate Canadian entry: Canadian environmental history is part of North American environmental history (user, 2026-10-12). Canadian scholars join the existing Environmental history entry.

open_questions: Missing groups? Business and economic history, legal history, urban history, history of education, Black Canadian history, public history and memory.
